results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** The simultaneous normalized matrices
$B_i^{(5)}\oplus B_i^{(8)}$, their common braid word $C$, and
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

[F1] The five-dimensional proof constructs 24 independent Lie words from
$X=C_5-C_5^{-1}$ and records determinant character $r^3$; the
eight-dimensional proof constructs 63 independent Lie words from
$X=C_8-C_8^{-1}$ and records determinant character $r^5$.
[[thm-qc-tqc-b6-su5-density]] [[thm-qc-tqc-b6-su8-density]]

[F2] Closed subgroups are Lie subgroups under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, and their
Lie algebras are bracket closed.
[[thm-cartans-closed-subgroup-theorem]]
[[prop-the-lie-algebra-of-a-lie-subgroup-is-a-lie-subalgebra]]

[F3] $\mathfrak{su}(5)$ and $\mathfrak{su}(8)$ have dimensions $24$ and
$63$ and consist of trace-zero skew-Hermitian matrices.
[[ex-unitary-and-special-unitary-lie-groups]]

[F4] Both $SU(5)$ and $SU(8)$ are connected.
[[lem-qc-tqc-special-unitary-connected]]

[A1] Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. [[def-countable-choice]]

[A2] Assume the fixed Fibonacci path convention and $F/R$ data stated in
[[lem-qc-tqc-fibonacci-b6-path-projectors-and-artin]].



1.1 The common Fibonacci data in [A2] give the same normalized two-dimensional three-strand block for $C=B_1B_2^{-1}$ in both total-charge spaces. Direct multiplication gives determinant $1$, trace $\phi^{-2}$, and eigenvalues $e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta}$ with $2\cos\theta=\phi^{-2}$ on that factor; the remaining factors contribute eigenvalue $1$. [A2, algebra]

1.2 For $n\ge2$, the complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)$ is simple. Let $I$ be a nonzero ideal. If some $X\in I$ has an off-diagonal entry $X_{ij}\ne0$, choose a traceless diagonal matrix $D$ whose ordered differences $\lambda_p-\lambda_q$ ($p\ne q$) are nonzero and pairwise distinct. Such a $D$ exists because each forbidden equality is a proper linear hyperplane in the trace-zero diagonal subspace, and finitely many proper hyperplanes do not cover a vector space over the infinite field $\mathbb C$. The map $\operatorname{ad}_D$ has eigenvectors $E_{pq}$ with these eigenvalues and is zero on diagonal matrices. Lagrange interpolation therefore supplies a polynomial in $\operatorname{ad}_D$ that sends $X$ to $X_{ij}E_{ij}$; since $I$ is an ideal, $E_{ij}\in I$. If instead a nonzero $X\in I$ is diagonal, it is nonscalar because it is traceless. Choose $i\ne j$ with $X_{ii}\ne X_{jj}$; then $[E_{ij},X]=(X_{jj}-X_{ii})E_{ij}\in I$, again giving a matrix unit. From $E_{ij}\in I$, bracketing with $E_{ji}$ gives $E_{ii}-E_{jj}\in I$, and bracketing that diagonal matrix with $E_{ji}$ gives $E_{ji}\in I$. For each $k\notin\{i,j\}$, $[E_{ki},E_{ij}]=E_{kj}$ and $[E_{jk},E_{ij}]=-E_{ik}$, so these units lie in $I$. Then $[E_{ji},E_{ik}]=E_{jk}$ for each such $k$. We now have $E_{kj}$ and $E_{jl}$ for every $k,l\ne j$; for $k\ne l$, $[E_{kj},E_{jl}]=E_{kl}$. Thus every off-diagonal matrix unit lies in $I$, and their brackets give all trace-zero diagonal matrices. Hence $I$ is the whole algebra. This also covers $n=2$, where the steps involving $k$ are empty. The complexification of $\mathfrak{su}(n)$ is $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)$: every traceless complex matrix is uniquely a sum $A+iB$ of traceless skew-Hermitian matrices. A nonzero real ideal of $\mathfrak{su}(n)$ would complexify to a nonzero ideal of $\mathfrak{sl}_n(\mathbb C)$, hence to all of it; equality of dimensions then makes the real ideal all of $\mathfrak{su}(n)$. Therefore $\mathfrak{su}(5)$ and $\mathfrak{su}(8)$ are simple. Their dimensions $24$ and $63$ from [F3] show they are not isomorphic. [F3, algebra]

2.1 The algebraic number $\phi^{-2}$ has minimal polynomial $x^2-3x+1$, whose other root is $\phi^2>2$. If $e^{i\theta}$ were a root of unity, every algebraic conjugate of $e^{i\theta}+e^{-i\theta}$ would be a sum of two roots of unity and have absolute value at most $2$. The conjugate $\phi^2>2$ contradicts this, so $\theta/(2\pi)$ is irrational. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The 24 independent Lie words in the five-dimensional proof and the deterministically selected 63 independent Lie words in the eight-dimensional proof are each formed from the initial tangent $X$ by conjugations by the same generators and Lie brackets. Applying those same word operations to $(X_5,X_8)$ gives elements of $\mathfrak g$ whose first projections span $\mathfrak{su}(5)$ and whose second projections span $\mathfrak{su}(8)$, respectively, by [F1]. Therefore both coordinate projections of $\mathfrak g$ are surjective. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Each normalized generator has determinant pair $(r^3,r^5)$ by the rank calculations in [F1]. The joint determinant image is therefore finite, so the identity component of the closure lies in $SU(5)\times SU(8)$ and $\mathfrak g\subseteq\mathfrak{su}(5)\oplus\mathfrak{su}(8)$. With both projections surjective by step 2.2, $\mathfrak g$ is a subdirect Lie subalgebra of that product. [F1, F2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Define the kernel ideals $K_5=\{x\in\mathfrak{su}(5):(x,0)\in\mathfrak g\}$ and $K_8=\{y\in\mathfrak{su}(8):(0,y)\in\mathfrak g\}$. They are ideals because $\mathfrak g$ projects onto both factors and is closed under brackets. Simplicity says each kernel is either zero or the whole factor. If either is the whole factor, surjectivity of the other projection implies $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(5)\oplus\mathfrak{su}(8)$. If both are zero, each projection restricts to an isomorphism from $\mathfrak g$ to its factor, yielding an isomorphism $\mathfrak{su}(5)\cong\mathfrak{su}(8)$, contrary to their different dimensions. Thus $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(5)\oplus\mathfrak{su}(8)$. [F2, F3, step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra]

5.1 By [F2], the identity component of the joint closure is an embedded Lie subgroup of $SU(5)\times SU(8)$ with this full Lie algebra. It has full dimension and is open. The product is connected by [F4], so that open subgroup is the entire product. Therefore the joint closure contains $SU(5)\times SU(8)$. The only choice assumption is [A1]. [A1, F2, F4, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The fixed-chirality Fibonacci $F/R$ data and the Artin presentation.

[A1] Assume every generator has the same scalar $R_1$ on all fusion
channels; its relative channel phases define the normalized generator. The
actual Fibonacci data carrier fixes $R_1=e^{-4\pi i/5}$ and
$R_\tau=e^{3\pi i/5}$ in its stated gauge.
[[ex-qc-tqc-fibonacci-data]]

[F2] Standalone unit-modulus phases leave pure-state measurement
probabilities unchanged.
[[thm-qc-standalone-global-phase-invariance]]

[F3] A separately controlled scalar phase can change measurement
probabilities by becoming relative to the control branch.
[[thm-qc-controlled-global-phase-is-relative-phase]]



1.1 Exponent sum is well defined on the Artin group: both sides of every adjacent braid relation have sum $3$, both sides of every distant commutation relation have sum $2$, and inverse cancellation changes the sum by $0$. Thus $e:B_n\to\mathbb Z$ is a homomorphism. [given, algebra]

2.1 For a word $b=\sigma_{i_1}^{\epsilon_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_k}^{\epsilon_k}$, each positive generator contributes $R_1$ and each inverse contributes $R_1^{-1}$ to the scalar, by [A1]. The scalar product is therefore $R_1^{\epsilon_1+\cdots+\epsilon_k}=R_1^{e(b)}$, while the remaining normalized matrices multiply to $\widetilde\rho(b)$. Since every relation preserves exponent sum, this factorization is independent of the word representative. [A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The same scalar multiplies every charge block, so [F2] applies to an uncontrolled isolated sector. Under coherent control the scalar multiplies only the active branch, and [F3] shows it becomes a relative phase; it cannot be discarded without recording or correcting it. [F2, F3, step 2.1] ∎

**Given:** The fixed Fibonacci fusion rule, the unitary fusion-tree bases, and
the chiral $F/R$ coordinates displayed in the Statement.

[F2] A fusion-tree basis retains each admissible intermediate charge and
vertex multiplicity index. The current supplier body was inspected.
[[def-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-basis]]

[A1] Assume the Fibonacci fusion rule and the fixed-chirality data displayed
in the Statement: the normalized pair-channel eigenvalues are $1,r$, and
the nontrivial recoupling block is the displayed $F$ matrix. The actual
Fibonacci data carrier states this fusion rule and these fixed sector
matrices. [[ex-qc-tqc-fibonacci-data]]



1.1 Starting with $(x_0,x_1)=(0,1)$, the fusion rule permits only $x_{j+1}=1$ when $x_j=0$, and permits $x_{j+1}\in\{0,1\}$ when $x_j=1$. Enumerating the five remaining transitions with endpoint $x_6=0$ or $1$ gives exactly the two path sets displayed in the Statement; hence the block dimensions are $5$ and $8$. Also $r^5=-1$ and $r\ne-1$, so $r^4-r^3+r^2-r+1=0$. For $y=r+r^{-1}$, division by $r^2$ gives $y^2-y-1=0$; since $y=2\cos(3\pi/5)<0$, $y=-\phi^{-1}$. Thus $r^2+\phi^{-1}r+1=0$. [given, A1, F2, construct, algebra]

1.2 In a fixed left-tree basis, $P_i$ is the projection onto pair channel $1$. The $F$-move gives the only nontrivial local block, on the two intermediate channels $(1,\tau)$: $$\begin{pmatrix}\phi^{-2}&\phi^{-3/2}\\ \phi^{-3/2}&\phi^{-1}\end{pmatrix}.$$ Its square equals itself because $\phi^{-4}+\phi^{-3}=\phi^{-2}$, $\phi^{-3/2}(\phi^{-2}+\phi^{-1})=\phi^{-3/2}$, and $\phi^{-3}+\phi^{-2}=\phi^{-1}$; its entries are real symmetric. When the surrounding charge is the unit, the only allowed pair-channel block is $[1]$. Thus each $P_i=P_i^*=P_i^2$. Counting the diagonal entries of these blocks on the listed paths gives $\operatorname{tr}P_i=2$ on $\mathcal P_1$ and $3$ on $\mathcal P_\tau$, so these are the ranks. [given, A1, F2, algebra]

1.3 On the nontrivial three-strand total-$\tau$ block, the adjacent projections are $P=|e_1\rangle\langle e_1|$ and $Q=|f_1\rangle\langle f_1|$, where $f_1=(\phi^{-1},\phi^{-1/2})$ is the first column of $F$. Therefore $PQP=|\langle e_1,f_1\rangle|^2P=\phi^{-2}P$ and symmetrically $QPQ=\phi^{-2}Q$. In the one-dimensional total-$1$ block both adjacent projections are zero, so the same identities hold. Tensoring with spectator path factors leaves these identities unchanged. Operators on disjoint pairs commute by the interchange law for tensor products. [A1, algebra]

2.1 Put $q_0=\phi^{-2}$. For adjacent $P=P_i,Q=P_{i+1}$ and $s=1-r$, direct expansion using $P^2=P$, $Q^2=Q$, $PQP=q_0P$, and $QPQ=q_0Q$ gives $$[rI+sP][rI+sQ][rI+sP]-[rI+sQ][rI+sP][rI+sQ] =s\bigl(r+q_0s^2\bigr)(P-Q).$$ Because $r+r^{-1}=-\phi^{-1}$, $\bigl(r+q_0(1-r)^2\bigr)/r =1+\phi^{-2}(r+r^{-1}-2) =1-\phi^{-2}(\phi^{-1}+2)=0$; here $\phi^{-1}+2=\phi^2$. Thus the adjacent braid relation holds. [A1, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Since $P_i$ is an orthogonal projection and $|r|=1$, $B_i$ acts by $1$ on $\operatorname{ran}P_i$ and by $r$ on its orthogonal complement, so it is unitary. The distant commutation and adjacent relation from steps 1.3–2.2 are the defining Artin relations, hence the matrices represent $B_6$. The rank table gives rank $2$ on the five-dimensional block and rank $3$ on the eight-dimensional block, so $\det B_i=r^{5-2}=r^3$ and $\det B_i=r^{8-3}=r^5$, respectively. [given, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The fixed Fibonacci root $r$, the golden ratio $\phi$, and the
positive square root $s=\sqrt\phi$.

[A1] Assume the fixed-chirality root $r=R_\tau/R_1=e^{-3\pi i/5}$ from the
actual Fibonacci data carrier; the positive square root $s=\sqrt\phi$ is
fixed in the Statement. The carrier states the phases
$R_1=e^{-4\pi i/5}$ and $R_\tau=e^{3\pi i/5}$.
[[ex-qc-tqc-fibonacci-data]]



1.1 The number $r$ is a primitive tenth root of unity, so its minimal polynomial is $\Phi_{10}(x)=x^4-x^3+x^2-x+1$ and $[\mathbb Q(r):\mathbb Q]=4$. Its maximal real subfield is $\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)$, and the nontrivial conjugate of $\phi$ is $(1-\sqrt5)/2=-\phi^{-1}$; hence the field norm of $\phi$ from $\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)$ to $\mathbb Q$ is $-1$. Therefore $\phi$ is not a square in that real subfield, since the norm of a square would be a nonnegative rational square. [given, A1, algebra]

2.1 If $u\in\mathbb Q(r)$ satisfied $u^2=\phi$, complex conjugation would give $\bar u^2=\phi$, hence $\bar u=u$ or $\bar u=-u$. In the first case $u\in\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)$, contradicting step 1.1. In the second case $u$ is purely imaginary in the chosen embedding, so $u^2$ is nonpositive real, contrary to $\phi>0$. Thus $Y^2-\phi$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q(r)$ and $[\mathbb Q(r,s):\mathbb Q]=8$. The displayed monic relations therefore give the full degree-eight presentation; no additional relation is being assumed. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 In $\mathbb F_{31}$, $15^{-1}=29$, $\Phi_{10}(15)=0$, $1-15-29=19$, and $9^2=19$. Thus the assignments satisfy both defining relations and extend to the stated ring homomorphism. The images $15$ and $19$ are nonzero, so $r,\phi$ and their powers are units; all denominators in the path projectors and normalized braid matrices are therefore invertible after specialization. [given, A1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 In the number field, complex conjugation fixes $\phi,s$ and sends $r$ to $r^{-1}$. Therefore a coefficient involving conjugation is first rewritten with $r^{-1}$ and only then reduced by $r^{-1}\mapsto29$. No conjugation operation on $\mathbb F_{31}$ is required. [given, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The projective unitary group $PU(2)$ with its quotient metric, the
matrix group $SU(2)$, and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

[F1] The projective distance is a metric and
$d_P([A],[B])=\min_{|z|=1}\|A-zB\|_{\mathrm{op}}$.
[[def-qc-tqc-projective-gate-and-metric]]

[F2] Closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are compact.
[[thm-heine-borel-rn]]

[F3] A compact subset of a Hausdorff space is closed.
[[thm-compact-subset-of-a-hausdorff-space-is-closed]]

[F4] Every unit complex number has the form $e^{i\theta}$ for some real
$\theta$. [[thm-sine-and-cosine-parametrize-the-unit-circle]]

[F5] Quaternionic conjugation gives a surjective two-sheeted covering
$\rho:SU(2)\to SO(3)$ with kernel $\{I,-I\}$.
[[ex-su-two-to-so-three-as-a-covering-homomorphism]]

[A1] Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the exact choice principle used by [F5].
[[def-countable-choice]]



1.1 The determinant of a unitary $A\in U(2)$ has modulus one, since $1=\det(A^*A)=\overline{\det A}\det A$. Write $\det A=e^{i\theta}$ by [F4] and put $\lambda=e^{-i\theta/2}$. Then $|\lambda|=1$ and $\det(\lambda A)=\lambda^2\det A=1$, so $\lambda A\in SU(2)$ and $q(\lambda A)=q(A)$. Thus $q$ is onto. [given, F4, algebra]

2.1 If $A\in SU(2)$ and $q(A)=[I]$, then $A=\lambda I$ for some $|\lambda|=1$. The determinant condition gives $\lambda^2=1$, hence $\lambda=\pm1$. Conversely $I$ and $-I$ have the same projective class. Therefore $\ker q=\{\pm I\}$, and two matrices have the same $q$-image exactly when they differ by this kernel. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The map $q$ is continuous: by [F1], $d_P(q(A),q(B))\le\|A-B\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Identify $M_2(\mathbb C)$ with $\mathbb R^8$. The equations $A^*A=I$ and $\det A=1$ define a closed subset, and each matrix entry is bounded in modulus by $1$ because each column has norm $1$. Thus $SU(2)$ is compact by [F2]. The metric space $PU(2)$ is Hausdorff by [F1]. If $F\subseteq SU(2)$ is closed, then it is compact and $q(F)$ is compact, hence closed by [F3]. It is a quotient map: if $q^{-1}(W)$ is open, then $q^{-1}(PU(2)\setminus W)$ is closed; surjectivity and closedness of $q$ make its image $PU(2)\setminus W$ closed, so $W$ is open. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F5] and step 2.1, $q$ and $\rho$ have exactly the same fibers. There is therefore a unique bijective group homomorphism $\bar\rho:PU(2)\to SO(3)$ with $\bar\rho(q(A))=\rho(A)$. It is continuous because $q$ is a quotient map and $\rho=\bar\rho\circ q$ is continuous. The space $PU(2)=q(SU(2))$ is compact, while $SO(3)$ is Hausdorff as a subspace of the real $3\times3$ matrix space. A continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism: images of closed sets are compact and therefore closed by [F3]. Hence $\bar\rho$ is a topological group isomorphism. Since $q$ is a quotient map and its fibers are exactly the cosets of $\{\pm I\}$ by step 2.1, the induced map $SU(2)/\{\pm I\}\to PU(2)$ is also a homeomorphism. The covering sheets for $q$ are carried from those of $\rho$ by this homeomorphism, so $q$ is a two-sheeted covering. [A1, F3, F5, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Finite-dimensional inner-product spaces $\mathcal C,V$, an
isometry $J:\mathcal C\to V$, a unitary $U$ on $\mathcal C$, a unitary $W$ on
$V$, and zero logical block error.

[F1] The logical block error is $\|PWP-JUJ^*\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ and the leakage
amplitude is $\|(I-P)WP\|_{\mathrm{op}}$; $P=JJ^*$ is the orthogonal
projection onto $J\mathcal C$.
[[def-qc-tqc-logical-error-and-leakage]]

[F2] Isometries preserve inner-product norm, and orthogonal projection splits
a vector into orthogonal code and complement components.
[[def-linear-isometry-and-orthogonal-or-unitary-operator]]
[[def-inner-product-norm]]



1.1 Zero block error means $PWP=JUJ^*$ as operators on $V$. For every $x\in\mathcal C$, $J^*J=I_{\mathcal C}$ gives $PWJx=PWPJx=JUJ^*Jx=JUx$. By [F2], $\|WJx\|=\|x\|$ and $\|PWJx\|=\|JUx\|=\|Ux\|=\|x\|$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The decomposition $WJx=PWJx+(I-P)WJx$ is orthogonal by [F1]. Its Pythagorean identity and step 1.1 give $\|(I-P)WJx\|^2=\|WJx\|^2-\|PWJx\|^2=0$ for every $x$. Hence $(I-P)WJ=0$, and since $P=JJ^*$, $(I-P)WP=0$; its operator norm is zero. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The Hopf coproduct, the two evaluation modules, and the rational spectral $R$-matrix with its spectral Yang–Baxter equation.

[F1] [[prop-yangian-gl-n-rtt-hopf-structure]]: $\Delta(T(u))=T^{[1]}(u)T^{[2]}(u)$ is a coassociative coproduct; applying the tensor flip to $\Delta$ reverses the two matrix factors.

[F2] [[thm-yangian-evaluation-module-well-defined]]: for any $\mathfrak{gl}_N$-module and parameter $c$, $t_{ij}(u)=\delta_{ij}-i\rho(E_{ij})/(u-c)$ defines a Yangian action; on $V_N^\vee$ its auxiliary Lax matrix is $R_N(u-c)$.

[F3] [[prop-yangian-rational-r-matrix-yang-baxter-and-invertibility]]: $R_{12}(x)R_{13}(x+y)R_{23}(y)=R_{23}(y)R_{13}(x+y)R_{12}(x)$, and $R_N(d)$ is invertible exactly when $d\notin\{i,-i\}$.

[F4] [[def-yangian-evaluation-module]]: $V_N^\vee(a)$ has the dual-natural action and its auxiliary series is $I+iP_N/(u-a)$, whose polynomial Lax matrix is $R_N(u-a)$.



1.1 On the same ordered space $W_a\otimes W_b$, the coproduct action has auxiliary matrix $T_0(u)=T_{0a}(u)T_{0b}(u)$ by [F1]. The opposite coproduct reverses those two matrix factors, giving $T_{0b}(u)T_{0a}(u)$. Multiplying both by the scalar $(u-a)(u-b)$ gives the polynomial products $L_{0a}(u-a)L_{0b}(u-b)$ and $L_{0b}(u-b)L_{0a}(u-a)$, since [F2] and [F4] give $L_{0c}(u-c)=R_{0c}(u-c)$ for $c=a,b$. [given, F1, F2, F4, algebra]

2.1 Apply the spectral Yang–Baxter identity [F3] on auxiliary space $0$ and quantum spaces $a,b$, using their indexed-basis identifications and spectral points $u,a,b$. It gives $L_{0a}(u-a)L_{0b}(u-b)R_{ab}(a-b)=R_{ab}(a-b)L_{0b}(u-b)L_{0a}(u-a)$. Since $(u-a)(u-b)$ is nonzero and invertible in the scalar Laurent-series field at infinity, cancel it from the two polynomial Lax products in step 1.1. The resulting identity is the claimed intertwining relation for $T_0(u)$, and equality of its matrix entries gives it for each $t_{ij}(u)$ coefficient. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $a-b\notin\{i,-i\}$, [F3] makes $R_{ab}$ invertible, so the intertwiner is an isomorphism. At $a-b=i$ its kernel is antisymmetric, and at $a-b=-i$ its kernel is symmetric, by [F3]; the identity in step 2.1 still holds because the Yang–Baxter identity is polynomial and no inverse was used. [given, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The RTT presentation for $N=2$, a representation, and a vector satisfying the displayed vacuum eigenvalue conditions.

[F1] [[lem-yangian-rtt-component-commutator-form]]: $x[t_{ij}(u),t_{kl}(v)]=i(t_{kj}(v)t_{il}(u)-t_{kj}(u)t_{il}(v))$ for $x=u-v$.



1.1 Apply [F1] to $(i,j,k,l)=(1,2,1,1)$ and interchange $u,v$; rearranging gives $A(u)B(v)=\frac{x-i}{x}B(v)A(u)+\frac{i}{x}B(u)A(v)$ for $x=u-v\ne0$. Applying [F1] to $(i,j,k,l)=(2,2,1,2)$ gives $D(u)B(v)=\frac{x+i}{x}B(v)D(u)-\frac{i}{x}B(u)D(v)$. All divisions are by the stated nonzero scalar $x$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Apply these identities to $\Omega$ and use its eigenvalue conditions. The coefficient of $B(u)\Omega$ in $(A(u)+D(u))B(v)\Omega$ is $i(a(v)-d(v))/x$, which vanishes under $a(v)=d(v)$. The remaining coefficient of $B(v)\Omega$ is exactly $\Lambda_v(u)$, so the claimed eigenvector identity follows; nonzero-ness of $B(v)\Omega$ makes it an eigenvector rather than merely a zero-vector identity. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A finite chain with the local Lax operators and order specified in [[def-yangian-periodic-fundamental-chain]], and the polynomial spectral Yang–Baxter identity.

[F1] [[def-yangian-periodic-fundamental-chain]]: $M_0(u)=\prod_{j=1}^m L_{0j}(u)$ in increasing site order, $L_{0j}(u)=R_{0j}(u-a_j)$, and different quantum sites are distinct tensor factors.

[F2] [[prop-yangian-rational-r-matrix-yang-baxter-and-invertibility]]: the polynomial $R$-matrix satisfies the spectral Yang–Baxter identity for all complex parameters.



1.1 On a fixed site $j$, apply [F2] to auxiliary spectral points $u,v$ and the site parameter $a_j$. By the indexed-basis convention of [F1], the local relation is $R_{00'}(u-v)L_{0j}(u)L_{0'j}(v)=L_{0'j}(v)L_{0j}(u)R_{00'}(u-v)$. If $j\ne k$, then $L_{0j}(u)$ and $L_{0'k}(v)$ act on disjoint auxiliary and quantum tensor factors, so their coefficients commute and their operators commute. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 Assume it holds for $m-1$, and write $M_0^{(m)}=M_0^{(m-1)}L_{0m}$ and $M_{0'}^{(m)}=M_{0'}^{(m-1)}L_{0'm}$. [IH, F1, given]

2.1 For $m=1$, the required equation is exactly step 1.1. [base, step 1.1]

3.1 Moving $L_{0m}$ past $M_{0'}^{(m-1)}$ is valid by step 1.1. The induction hypothesis gives $R M_0^{(m)}M_{0'}^{(m)}=M_{0'}^{(m-1)}M_0^{(m-1)}R L_{0m}L_{0'm}$. Apply the local relation at site $m$, then commute $L_{0'm}$ past $M_0^{(m-1)}$ because they act on distinct sites. The result is $M_{0'}^{(m)}M_0^{(m)}R$, proving the induction step and the claim for every finite $m$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, induction, discharge-induction: step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The two-auxiliary-leg RTT matrix relation with $R_N(x)=xI+iP_N$.

[F1] [[def-yangian-gl-n-rtt-presentation]]: $R_N(x)=xI+iP_N$ with the auxiliary flip $P_N(e_a\otimes e_b)=e_b\otimes e_a$, and $R_{12}(u-v)T_1(u)T_2(v)=T_2(v)T_1(u)R_{12}(u-v)$.



1.1 In the coefficient of the auxiliary row $(i,k)$ and column $(j,l)$, the $xI$ part of the left side is $x t_{ij}(u)t_{kl}(v)$ and the $iP$ part is $i t_{kj}(u)t_{il}(v)$, because the flip sends the row $(i,k)$ to $(k,i)$. On the right side the corresponding terms are $x t_{kl}(v)t_{ij}(u)$ and $i t_{kj}(v)t_{il}(u)$, since the flip acts on the column. Thus equality of those matrix entries gives $x t_{ij}(u)t_{kl}(v)+i t_{kj}(u)t_{il}(v)=x t_{kl}(v)t_{ij}(u)+i t_{kj}(v)t_{il}(u)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Subtract the two $x$-terms and move the two $i$-terms to the other side. The result is exactly the displayed commutator relation.
